anchors.paper_title: The Role of Rapid Eye Movement Sleep in Neural Differentiation of Memories in the Hippocampus
anchors.reason: The dataset README cites this exact paper (McDevitt, Kim, Turk-Browne, Norman, JOCN) as the source of the fMRI and EEG data, with matching title and authors.

metadata.methods_description: Data collection included three fMRI scans and one EEG session per participant. The EEG session recorded either sleep (nap) or quiet wake data depending on the participant's assigned condition. Participants also completed behavioral tasks including a decision task and a reward prediction task during fMRI sessions.

citation_details.title: Pre-sleep experiences shape neural activity and dream content in the sleeping brain
citation_details.author: Deniz Kumral, Jessica Palmieri, Steffen Gais, Monika Schönauer
citation_details.abstract: Dreams incorporate recent experiences, and memory-related brain activity is reactivated during sleep, suggesting that dreaming, memory consolidation, and reactivation are tightly linked. We devised a paradigm to investigate whether memory reprocessing during sleep contributes to dreaming. Participants listened to different audiobooks before falling asleep, introducing dissimilar experiences to be processed at night. We show that audiobook content was reprocessed at the neural level using multivariate pattern analyses. Brain activity during rapid eye movement sleep, particularly in the beta range, carried information about the audiobook. While the amount of neural reinstatement did not correlate with memory retention, global beta power during REM sleep was associated with better memory performance. citation_details.title: Adaptive processing of predictions and prediction errors in hippocampal subregions
citation_details.author: Oded Bein, Lila Davachi
citation_details.venue: Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B Biological Sciences
citation_details.abstract: The hippocampus is central to generating memory-based predictions and responding when reality matches or violates these predictions. Here, we examine fMRI research of hippocampal subregions in humans and identify distinct putative mechanisms underlying such predictive processing. Specifically, hippocampal regions CA3 and CA1 may both support predictive processing, but at different stages of learning. Emerging evidence supports the view that CA3 can represent memory-based predictions by pattern-completing the prediction from a cue after only minimal learning. CA1 predictive representations, however, may emerge when predictions are well learnt; CA1, thus, might serve as a 'gatekeeper' that relays established predictions to downstream regions. Through pattern separation, the dentate gyrus may support fine-grained, immediate predictions that distinguish similar events. citation_details.title: Imperatorin restores behavioral and recognition memory deficits induced by REM sleep deprivation in male rats
citation_details.author: Mohammad Mojtaba Ayati, Maryam Eslami, Batool Ghorbani Yekta
citation_details.abstract: Many studies have shown the deleterious effects of rapid-eye movement (REM) sleep deprivation (SD) on cognitive functions and synaptic plasticity markers. On the other hand, imperatorin (IMP, extracted from the fruits of Angelica dahurica and Peucedanum praeruptorum) may exert significant pro-cognitive and neuroprotective effects. The present study aimed to explore the potential therapeutic effects of IMP on behavioral and molecular changes induced by REM SD, before or after training in the novel object recognition (NOR) memory test. REM SD was done for 24 h and IMP was orally administered at the dose of 100 mg/kg (immediately after REM SD). Locomotion, anxiety-like behavior, and brain-derived neurotrophic factor (BDNF) and cAMP response element binding (CREB) levels were also assessed in the prefrontal cortex. citation_details.title: Gravity in the Eye: How ‘Gravitational Ischemia’ in the Retina May Be Released and Resolved Through Rapid Eye Movement (REM), a Component of Gravity Opposition Physiology
citation_details.author: J. Howard Jaster, Joshua Ong, Giulia Ottaviani, MD, PhD
citation_details.abstract: This narrative review of rapid eye movement (REM) focuses on its primary etiology and how it fits into the larger framework of neurophysiology and general physiology. Arterial blood flow in the retina may be sensitive to the full overlying ‘weight’ of its adjacent and contiguous vitreous humor caused by the humoral mass effect in the Earth’s gravitational field. During waking hours of the day, this ‘weight’ is continuously shifted in position due to changing head position and eye movements associated with ordinary environmental observations. This reduces its impact on any one point on the retinal field. However, during sleep, the head may maintain a relatively constant position (often supine), and observational eye movements are minimal, leaving essentially one retinal area exposed at the ‘bottom’ of each eye, relative to gravity. citation_details.title: Dynamic thresholds and spatial boundaries coordinate memory association and discrimination across scales
citation_details.author: Yujun Luo, Lu Yang, Shuaizhu Zhao, Xinyue Nan, Jun Yang, Tongmei Zhang, Hao Li
citation_details.abstract: The ability to connect related experiences while preserving their individual identities is a central requirement of adaptive behavior. Engram overlap offers a cellular substrate for memory linking, but overlap must be regulated: too little prevents integration, whereas too much promotes generalization, interference, and confusion. Here, we organize evidence across molecular, cellular, glial, circuit, and systems levels around a common association-discrimination problem. We distinguish prospective linking, in which temporally adjacent experiences are biased toward shared neuronal allocation during a transient excitability window, from retrospective linking, in which memories separated in time are integrated through replay and cross-regional coordination. citation_details.title: Firing Without Wiring: How REM-like Sleep Reactivation Rebalances Excitation and Inhibition to Orthogonalize Memories
citation_details.author: Yoshimasa Kubo, Erik Delanois, Bazhenov Maxim
citation_details.abstract: The role of Rapid Eye Movement (REM) sleep in memory consolidation remains poorly understood. Several influential ideas propose that REM sleep serves to eliminate crosstalk between memories, thereby orthogonalizing representations of similar ones; however, mechanistic confirmation remains sparse. Here we used recurrent neural networks trained with Equilibrium Propagation (EP), a biologically plausible training algorithm, to investigate the role of REM-like sleep in memory consolidation. We found that REM-like sleep reduces memory interference by decorrelating task-specific neuronal populations, isolating individual memory traces. During sleep, reactivation was dominated by the population encoding the most recent memory, which had taken over the inputs of older memories during new learning. The excitation/inhibition balance of inputs onto this population shifted toward inhibition, most strongly from older-memory populations, so that older memories again activated their own neurons. citation_details.title: Closed-loop Auditory Stimulation of Sleep Slow Oscillations: Basic Principles and Best Practices.
citation_details.author: M. J. Esfahani, S. Farboud, Hong-Viet V. Ngo, Jules Schneider, F. D. Weber, L. Talamini, M. Dresler
citation_details.abstract: Sleep is essential for our physical and mental well-being. During sleep, despite the paucity of overt behavior, our brain remains active and exhibits a wide range of coupled brain oscillations. In particular slow oscillations are characteristic for sleep, however whether they are directly involved in the functions of sleep, or are mere epiphenomena, is not yet fully understood. To disentangle the causality of these relationships, experiments utilizing techniques to detect and manipulate sleep oscillations in real time are essential. In this review, we first overview the theoretical principles of closed-loop auditory stimulation (CLAS) as a method to study the role of slow oscillations in the functions of sleep. We then describe technical guidelines and best practices to perform CLAS and analyze results from such experiments.
